summary: Max Weber was a scholar in religious studies, philosophy, and other fields who studied at Heidelberg, Strasbourg, Berlin, and Göttingen. He held posts at Freiburg (~1894–1896), Heidelberg (~1896–1903), Vienna (~1918), and Munich (~1919–1920).
Maximilian Bittner worked in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the University of Vienna (~1888–1892) under Friedrich Müller and later taught Robert Bleichsteiner.
Maximilian Enger was an Indologist who earned his Ph.D. from the University of Bonn (~1847–1851). He subsequently served as a Privatdozent at the University of Bonn from 1852 to 1861.

Maximilian Hoth works in Indology and Buddhist studies. He earned an MA at the University of Hamburg (2023–2025), is attested as a doctoral candidate at the Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities (2026), and held a PhD candidate post at Munich in 2026.
May Oung was active in history and archaeology, having studied at the University of Cambridge (~1904–1907). He founded the Burma Research Society in 1910.

Maya Jasanoff is a historian who studied at Harvard College, Cambridge, and Yale. She held a post at the University of Virginia (~2003–2009) and became a professor of history at Harvard University around 2009.
Maya Keller-Grimm worked in Buddhist studies. Between approximately 1948 and 1989, she served as the leader of the Altbuddhistische Gemeinde and worked as an editor for Yāna.
Mayum Chonying Wangmo Dorji was active in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She founded the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology and served as a General Council member there from 1964 to 1965.

Mayumi Nasu is a scholar in Buddhist studies and history/archaeology. She held a post as a lecturer at Shuchiin University (attested 2011–2013) and as a specially appointed associate professor at Koyasan University (attested 2026).

Małgorzata Sulich-Cowley works in Indology, linguistics, and philosophy, having studied at Pune, Lausanne, and Warsaw (PhD 2006–2013). She was a teaching associate at SWPS University (2015) and a research assistant at the University of Warsaw (2018–2021).
McComas Taylor is an Indologist who completed a PhD at the Australian National University. He held an emeritus professor post there in 2005.

McKim Marriott was a scholar of Indology and religious studies who studied at Harvard, under Clyde Kluckhohn, and at the University of Chicago (PhD ~1948–1955). He served as a professor at the University of Chicago (~1955–1998).

Md Mohiuddin Ahmed Tanvir completed a BA at the University of Dhaka (2019–2023) in Buddhist and religious studies. He worked as a counsellor at AHZ Bangladesh (2024–2025), IDP Education (2025–2026), and Kampus Group (2026).

Medawachchiye Dhammajothi works in Buddhist studies and Indology, holding degrees from Sri Jayewardenepura, PGIPBS, and Nanjing University. In 2008, he held posts at the University of Colombo, Buddhist and Pali University of Sri Lanka, and PGIPBS.
Medhani studied under Penor Rinpoche and Dudjom Rinpoche.

Megan Bryson is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. She earned her PhD from Stanford University (2002–2010) and served as an associate professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville (attested 2017).

Megumu Honda was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Johannes Rahder (1961–1962), Paul Tedesco, and Rulon Wells. He held a post as a professor at Doho University (attested 1996).

Mei Ching Hsuan works in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, having earned a PhD at the University of Bonn under Peter Schwieger and Dieter Schuh. As of 2026, she is attested as a professor at Chung-Hwa Institute of Buddhist Studies.
Meiji Yamada is an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Ryukoku University (attested 1962). He also served as a professor at Ryukoku University (attested 1963–1971 and 2007).

Meinrad Scheller was a linguist and Indologist who studied under Leumann, Pokorny, and Risch, completing his Dr. phil. and Habilitation at Zurich. He held professorships at Fribourg (1963), Munich (1968–1975), and Zurich (1975–1988).
